title: Taking root and reaping rewards
subtitle: plant and gardening metaphors
summary: Use the language of seeds, roots, branches and gardening figuratively to talk about origins, growth, success and decline.

lesson.heading: Seeds and roots: where things begin
lesson.text: A **seed** is literally the tiny thing a plant grows from, so figuratively it is the start of an idea or a feeling. A **root** is literally what holds a plant in the ground and feeds it, so figuratively it is the origin of something, or the place a family comes from.

examples.text: His grandfather sowed the **seeds** of the business's success.
examples.note: the seeds of success, the seeds of discontent, the seeds of revolution

examples.text: Nobody has asked what the **root of the problem** actually is.
Alec has spent his life in London, but he wants to go back to his **roots** in Scotland when he retires.
After travelling the world for a couple of years, I was ready to go home and **put down some roots**.
examples.note: put down roots = settle and make your home in one place

lesson.heading: Taking root, rooted, grassroots
lesson.text: When an idea becomes known and accepted, it **takes root**, just as a young plant does. When something has been in a place or a period for a very long time, it is **rooted** there - the adverbs **deeply** and **firmly** are the usual collocates. The **grassroots** supporters of an organisation are the ordinary members, not the leaders.

examples.text: The idea took some time to **take root**, but it is very fashionable now.
Its origins are **firmly rooted** in the 19th century.
The business is **firmly rooted** in Western Australia.
The party wants to reflect the views of its **grassroots** supporters.

lesson.note: Deeply rooted goes naturally with prejudice, hatred and tradition.

lesson.heading: Stems, buds and branches
lesson.text: The **stem** carries a plant upwards from its root, so **to stem from** something means to originate in it. A **bud** is a flower before it opens, so **to nip something in the bud** is to stop it before it develops, and **budding** describes someone showing promise. A **branch** grows off the main trunk, so a branch is an office or shop that grows off a main organisation.

examples.text: Her discontent **stems from** a traumatic experience she had last year.
The idea for her novel **stemmed from** her interest in mountain climbing.
He's showing signs of neglecting his work - we'd better **nip that in the bud**.

examples.note: budding = showing promise of future development

examples.text: We don't have the blue sweater in your size here, but you could try our Oxford Street **branch**.
The business is **branching out** into new directions.

lesson.heading: Gardening verbs used figuratively
rows: The new boss is planning to weed out less experienced staff.
The government will have to prune back its proposals.
At last she is reaping the rewards of all her years of study.
experience the logical results of your actions
Because we didn't protest, we are now reaping what we sowed.
The journalists have dug up some interesting facts.
The idea was germinating while we were on holiday.
Out-of-town shopping centres have been sprouting up all over the country.
lesson.note: Reap what you sowed is almost always negative - you are suffering the consequences of what you did.

lesson.heading: Growth and health vs decline and death

left.label: Growth and health
left.text: These verbs say something is doing well.
examples: Our business is **flourishing**. [is doing very well]
The language school is **thriving** - student numbers are up from last year.
She seems to **thrive on** stress and crises!
We are beginning to see the **green shoots** of economic recovery.

right.label: Decline and death
right.text: Plants fade, wither, shrivel and wilt when they die, and so do hopes, profits and people.
examples: Hopes of finding survivors are **fading**. [becoming smaller]
Revenues have **shrivelled** in recent years. [become less]
It was so hot in the classroom that the students were starting to **wilt**. [lose energy]
She gave him a **withering** look. [one that makes the other person feel scorned]

lesson.heading: Shedding
lesson.text: A deciduous tree **sheds** its leaves, meaning it loses them. Companies can **shed** employees or jobs, and people can **shed** worries, inhibitions or weight. The word suggests getting rid of something you no longer need or want.

examples.text: The firm has **shed** two hundred jobs this year.
She **shed** her inhibitions at the party and danced with everyone!
He's hoping to **shed** a few kilos before the wedding.

lesson.text: These metaphors are alive in everyday English: a business puts down roots, branches out, flourishes, then has to prune back and shed staff - one plant, a whole company history.

exercises.prompt: Match up the pairs to make collocations.
Alec has spent most of his life in London, but he is keen to get back to his ___ when he retires. His family came from Scotland, so he'll move there.
exercises.explanation: Go back to your roots = return to the place your family came from.

exercises.prompt: The business is firmly ___ in Western Australia.
exercises.explanation: Firmly and deeply are the usual adverbs with rooted.

exercises.prompt: The idea took some time to ___ root, but it's very fashionable now.
exercises.explanation: An idea takes root when it becomes known and accepted.

exercises.prompt: His grandfather sowed the ___ of the business's success.
exercises.explanation: You sow the seeds of something when you create its beginning.

exercises.prompt: The US bookshop chain is opening a number of ___ in the UK.
exercises.explanation: A branch grows off the main organisation, like a branch off a trunk.

exercises.prompt: It's about time she ___ down some roots.
exercises.explanation: Put down roots = settle and make your home in one place.

exercises.prompt: The idea for her novel ___ from her interest in mountain climbing.
exercises.explanation: Something stems from its origin, as a stem grows from a root.

exercises.prompt: The West Side Drama College turns out a hundred ___ actors every year.
exercises.explanation: Budding = showing promise of future development.

exercises.prompt: Is each verb associated with growth and health, or with decline and death?
Which noun goes most naturally with *withering*?
exercises.explanation: A withering glance, expression or remark makes the other person feel scorned.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with a plant metaphor: *The firm is cutting the labour force in order to reduce costs.*
options: The firm is **pruning back** the labour force in order to reduce costs.
The firm is **germinating** the labour force in order to reduce costs.
The firm is **sprouting up** the labour force in order to reduce costs.
The firm is **branching out** the labour force in order to reduce costs.
exercises.explanation: Prune back = cut or limit something, as you cut back a bush.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with a plant metaphor: *The party is trying hard to get rid of the extremists.*
options: The party is trying hard to **weed out** the extremists.
The party is trying hard to **dig up** the extremists.
The party is trying hard to **shed light on** the extremists.
The party is trying hard to **nip** the extremists.
exercises.explanation: Weed out = get rid of the unwanted members, as a gardener pulls out weeds.

exercises.statement: *Some people seem to thrive on difficult challenges* means that difficulties make them grow and develop.
exercises.explanation: To thrive on something is to grow and develop well because of it.

exercises.statement: *Don't be surprised if you reap what you sow* is usually said as a compliment.
exercises.explanation: Reap what you sow is almost always negative: you suffer the logical consequences of your own actions.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order. (A blogger discovered alarming facts.)
exercises.answer: A blogger dug up some alarming facts about government spending.
exercises.explanation: Dig up = discover, especially something hidden.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order. (We can see the first signs of recovery.)
exercises.answer: We are beginning to see the green shoots of an economic recovery.
exercises.explanation: Green shoots = the first signs that the economy is improving.
